title: Make String a Subsequence Using Cyclic Increments
statement:
You get two strings of lowercase letters, `str1` and `str2`. You may perform a single move, or no move at all: choose any set of positions in `str1` (possibly empty, possibly all of them) and advance the letter at each chosen position by one step in the alphabet, where `'z'` wraps around to `'a'`.

Return `true` when some such choice turns `str1` into a string that contains `str2` as a subsequence, and `false` otherwise. A subsequence keeps some of the characters (possibly all) in their original order and drops the rest.
constraints: str1 and str2 contain only lowercase English letters
notes:
## Intuition

Each character of `str1` can independently stay as it is or move one letter forward, because the single move may pick any set of positions. So a character of `str1` can stand in for a character of `str2` when it equals it or when its next letter (with `'z'` going to `'a'`) equals it. Trying every set of positions would cost O(2ⁿ); instead, this is the ordinary "is subsequence" check with a looser match rule, and matching greedily as early as possible never hurts.

## Approach

1. Keep `j`, the number of characters of `str2` already matched.
2. Walk `str1` with `i`, stopping early once all of `str2` is matched.
3. Compute the `current` code and its `shifted` code, wrapping `'z'` to `'a'`.
4. If either equals the `wanted` character `str2[j]`, use this character for it and advance `j`.
5. Return whether `j` reached the end of `str2`.

## Example 1, step by step

`str1 = "abc"`, `str2 = "ad"`. At `i = 0`, `'a'` equals the wanted `'a'`, so `j` becomes 1. At `i = 1`, `'b'` and its shift `'c'` both differ from `'d'`, so nothing happens. At `i = 2`, `'c'` shifts to `'d'`, a match, so `j` becomes 2, which equals the length of `str2`; the answer is `true`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): each character of `str1` is looked at once.
- Space: O(1): only a few counters and codes.

## Pitfalls

- Forgetting the wrap: `'z'` must also match `'a'`, not a character past `'z'`.
- A character may only move forward: `'b'` can become `'c'` but never `'a'`.
- Do not stop at the first mismatch; skipping characters of `str1` is what a subsequence allows.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `i` | position in `str1` |
| `j` | how many characters of `str2` are matched so far |
| `current` | character code of `str1[i]` |
| `shifted` | character code after one cyclic increment |
| `wanted` | character code of `str2[j]`, the next one to match |

narration.2: j counts how many characters of str2 are already matched.
narration.3: Scan str1 left to right, stopping once str2 is fully matched.
narration.4: Read the current character of str1 as a code.
narration.5: Its one-step increment, where 'z' (122) wraps to 'a' (97).
narration.6: The character of str2 we need next.
narration.7: The character works if it already matches or matches after one increment.
narration.8: Use it for str2[j] and move on to the next needed character.
narration.11: str2 is a subsequence exactly when every one of its characters was matched.
